Privacy & architecture
Where data lives, who can access it, and what the network exposes.

  

    
Connection privacy
—
Connection privacy changes routes. It does not change who can decrypt the room, recall shared links, or make you anonymous to the infrastructure carrying your connection. Global storage has its own anonymous-offering setting; room privacy also restricts its direct routes.

    
A browser application in one index.html
The application interface and peer logic are delivered as a single index.html. Your browser runs that code locally. The static page host supplies the application; this deployment has no central room account database, plaintext file catalog, or file-upload endpoint for participants’ content. Choosing a file makes your browser a source for peers; it does not upload that file to the web server hosting this page.
Single-file delivery does not mean offline or dependency-free operation. The page imports networking, media, model-viewing and transcoding libraries and assets from external CDNs, and connects to public rendezvous and relay services. Those services have their own operators and policies. Some file bytes travel through encrypted relays rather than a direct device-to-device connection.
Static host → application code → your browserYour disk / browser cache ↔ encrypted peer routes ↔ recipient browserOpt-in retention → encrypted browser copies / IPFS blocks / global provider blobs

    
Agent access and delegated windows
Public discovery describes commands only. Runtime resources require local approval and current command scopes. The local JavaScript and document-event interfaces act as the page agent; this is not isolation from other same-origin scripts. An independently approved window receives a separate principal, exact-origin/source binding and private nonce, restricted to this room and its selected scopes. It can read authorized room metadata and transfer bytes without receiving the room secret unless you explicitly grant link export. Native file, screen, microphone and camera inputs still need their own permissions. Binding policies and accepted jobs are encrypted in this browser. Window references and nonces are temporary; reconnecting after reload requires approval. Revoking a binding stops its active work; it cannot erase bytes already received or recall previously exported links. Filenames and peer content are untrusted data, never instructions or authority.

    
Room links are access credentials
A generated room link contains a random room secret in the URL fragment, after #. The room hash identifies a rendezvous namespace; the secret derives the room encryption key. Knowing the public hash or a file’s content hash alone does not grant decryption access. People without the secret cannot normally read the encrypted room catalog or file traffic.
Anyone who obtains the exact room link, or its secret through another means, can access that room’s shared catalog and request available ordinary files. There is no identity check proving the bearer is the person you intended. A file link contains the same room secret plus a file locator: it opens that file, but is not a file-only permission. Treat both kinds of link, and their QR codes, as credentials for the room.
People in one room do not automatically receive the secrets for other rooms. Default rooms allow room members to publish their own records. Protected rooms can restrict publishing to authorized signing identities; those write permissions do not hide ordinary files from people who already have the room secret. Separately password-locked files require their password to reveal their encrypted content and private file metadata.
The fragment is not sent in the ordinary HTTP request that retrieves this page. JavaScript running in the page can read it, and browser history, clipboard tools, screenshots, extensions, or recent-room entries can expose it. A forwarded, leaked or published link gives its new bearer the same room capability. URL fragment handling: RFC 3986 §3.5.

    
Where your data lives

      
Original files and live capture
Original files remain on the disk you choose. The browser holds a temporary file reference or, where supported and permitted, a saved file handle. It cannot silently browse your entire disk. Camera, microphone and screen capture require browser permission and an explicit sharing action. Viewers can record or save what they receive.

      
Room state and downloads
Room catalogs, signatures, preferences, resumable jobs and cached chunks live in the browser’s IndexedDB databases. Room KV records and cached file chunks are encrypted using the room key. Recent room links and some local preferences or relay identities are saved in browser local storage. Saved downloads also exist wherever the recipient saves them on disk. Explicit download exports may stage plaintext output in this device’s browser filesystem; Browser storage lists these separately and lets you remove them. These exports are separate from encrypted room caches and provider retention.

      
Agent access
Agent commands are disabled until you approve their local command scopes in Settings & identity. Commands use the same verification, signed catalog operations and peer routes as the interface. Additional rooms run in a bounded set of same-origin peer frames. Accepted jobs and operation receipts are encrypted in the room’s local IndexedDB database; selected File objects, password references and live captures are temporary inputs. A restarted job can require you to supply those inputs again. Revoking command access does not revoke a room link or isolate malicious JavaScript running under this site’s origin. Browser capture and native file permissions still require their own consent.

      
Playback and conversion
Playback uses decrypted data in browser memory and temporary streaming chunks. Compatibility conversion can create temporary plaintext inputs in the browser’s origin-private filesystem. Cleanup is attempted when work finishes and abandoned jobs are detected; a crash or browser behavior can leave temporary data until cleanup runs. “Ephemeral streaming” does not prevent recipients from recording, copying or retaining content.

      
Optional retained copies
Room retention creates verified browser copies on participating peers. IPFS pins use room-encrypted blocks and an encrypted index. Global retention puts additional room-encrypted objects and encrypted recovery metadata in providers’ browsers. These copies are separate from the original disk file and may outlive the uploader’s tab.

    

    
What different nodes can see

      
Participants with the room secret
Can decrypt room metadata, see ordinary filenames and sizes, publishing identities, availability and retention information, and request available files or live streams. A source can observe requests and traffic from room pseudonyms. Ordinary room retention providers are room participants and have this access too.
They do not automatically receive passwords for separately locked files or secrets for other rooms. Node signatures identify keys and attribute actions; they do not verify someone’s real-world identity or the legality of content.

      
Global bulk storage providers
Receive opaque object IDs, encrypted chunks, encrypted recovery metadata, object sizes and chunk counts, retention deadlines, a global provider/client pseudonym, and request timing. The global storage protocol does not send them the room secret, room hash, plaintext catalog, filename, or canonical file root.
Without separately obtaining the room secret or compromising an endpoint, they cannot decrypt those stored objects. A provider who is separately invited into the room becomes a room participant with the access described above. Encryption does not hide object sizes, traffic patterns or correlation opportunities.

      
Relay, rendezvous and routing operators
Handle discovery, control messages or encrypted bytes. Depending on the carrier they can observe source IP addresses, connections, routing topics or room identifiers, pseudonyms, message sizes, timing and ciphertext. Brokers or event relays may retain ciphertext or logs according to their own policies; this application cannot enforce their deletion.
They are not sent room decryption keys through the normal protocol. NATS, MQTT and Nostr can carry encrypted control and file/live bytes. WebRTC, NKN and libp2p offer other routes when permitted. Waku carries room control/discovery; IPFS stores and serves encrypted pinned blocks.

      
Direct peers, host and software suppliers
Direct peer connections can expose network addresses through connection setup. Relay-only privacy disables direct routes and restricts WebRTC to relay candidates where configured, reducing address exposure to peers. Broker, TURN, CDN, hosting and network operators still see the connections made to them.
The static host ordinarily receives page/asset requests and associated request metadata, not peer file uploads or the URL fragment. However, the host can change future application code. Imported scripts, a compromised origin, browser extensions or a compromised device can read accessible page data or misuse keys. You must trust the code you execute; a single HTML file is not a guarantee against malicious code.

    

    
Encryption, verification and availability
The current protocol uses room AES-GCM encryption, signed control/catalog records, authenticated transfer sessions and complete-file content-root verification. Password locking adds a separate file key. Completed transfers are verified before a cached copy becomes a source; streaming may play provisional bytes before complete-file verification. Integrity checks do not establish authorship by a real person, safety, permission to distribute, or legal compliance.
Peers and providers must be reachable to serve copies. Closing browsers, clearing storage, quota eviction, provider failure or expiry can make files unavailable. Retention is voluntary and best effort, not a backup guarantee. Keep independent backups of important data.

    
Sharing, deletion and control
You choose which files, live sources, links and storage allocations to make available. Stop capture to end a live source; pause or stop transfers and disable seeding to stop serving from this browser. Use Browser storage to inspect and clear local copies. Removing a file listing or your cache does not erase another person’s download, recordings, logs, retained objects or previously learned keys.
A leaked room secret cannot be taken back from its holders. Removing a write grant does not revoke their decryption key or erase copies they already have. Use a new room and stop sharing from the old one when you need a different audience; already distributed material remains outside your control.

    
Inspect the implementation
Download source saves the current deployed index.html, fetched from this site without your room fragment or query parameters. It does not export your browser databases, files, identities, keys or room link. A saved source file may be newer than an already-open tab and still relies on external libraries and network services. Serve it over HTTPS or localhost for browser cryptography and storage APIs.
Each participant is responsible for the content and permissions they choose to share, receive, retain or relay. The Disclaimer explains responsibilities, jurisdictional limits and the cited legal framework.

  

  



  
Disclaimer & responsibility
Participant obligations, the role of the static host, and legal limits.

  

    
A technical demonstration for lawful use
This application is a demonstration of browser-based encrypted peer communication and voluntary distributed storage, delivered as a static index.html. It is provided for lawful sharing of material you are entitled to distribute. It is not permission to infringe rights, expose private information without authority, evade legal obligations or engage in unlawful conduct.
Providing the application file is distinct from a participant selecting and exposing files or live media from their own machine. The static-page host does not choose participants’ files, recipients, room secrets or storage contents, and does not approve or endorse shared material. Under the normal application architecture, participant file bytes and private room catalogs are held by participants or encrypted storage providers rather than uploaded to the static host.

    
Your responsibility for your actions
You are responsible for what you choose to publish, transmit, stream, download, retain or re-share, for the people to whom you give access credentials, and for the devices, accounts and permissions you control. Confirm that you have the necessary rights, licenses, authorizations and consents before making material available. Receiving a room link is not proof that its contents are lawful or that you have permission to redistribute them.
That responsibility includes copyright and other intellectual property; confidentiality and contractual duties; personal-data and privacy obligations; recording and communications consent; prohibited content; and any applicable restrictions on cross-border transfers, encryption, export or sanctions. Screen sharing can expose other people’s messages, documents and credentials. Review the source and obtain required consent before sharing.
You must understand and comply with the laws of the jurisdictions in which you reside and operate, and other laws that validly apply to your activity. Peers, recipients, storage providers and infrastructure may be in different jurisdictions. Encryption, pseudonyms, a private link, a free service or decentralized routing do not make an unlawful act lawful or remove legal accountability.

    
Responsibility follows each participant’s role
A publisher decides which content to expose and to whom. A recipient decides what to request, save, record or distribute onward. A storage contributor chooses whether to retain or relay copies. A global provider normally holds opaque ciphertext without the room key; an ordinary room provider has the room’s access capability. Technical inability to read a blob is not a universal legal exemption.
Authors and the static-page operator do not assume responsibility for participants’ independent choices merely by supplying this demonstration. Each actor remains responsible for their own conduct and any duties imposed on their actual role. This allocation does not excuse an author, host or intermediary’s own unlawful conduct, bind third parties or public authorities, or override applicable law.

    
Access and persistence you need to understand
A room link and a file link both carry the room secret. Bearers can access that room’s catalog and available ordinary files; file links are not limited-access invitations to a single file. A separate password is needed for password-locked content. Recipients may forward links, copy files or record streams. A source can stop future serving from its own browser, but cannot recall information already disclosed or force every remote copy to disappear.
Data may live on source disks, receiving devices, encrypted browser caches, voluntary room retainers, encrypted IPFS pins or anonymous global storage providers. Relays and hosts can observe connection metadata, and may keep logs or ciphertext. The Privacy explanation gives the full architecture and visibility breakdown. Do not rely on this demonstration as your only backup or as a guarantee of secrecy, anonymity, availability or deletion.

    
Legal framework and its limits
The following sources illustrate relevant legal distinctions. They are not an exhaustive statement of the law, a determination that this deployment qualifies for a protection, or a legal opinion for any participant’s jurisdiction. The rules that apply depend on actual conduct, the service’s role, applicable law and satisfaction of any conditions.

      
United States: third-party information
47 U.S.C. §230(c)(1), (e) and (f) addresses when qualifying services or users are treated as publishers of another content provider’s information. Its exceptions include federal criminal law, intellectual property, communications privacy and specified trafficking matters. It is not a general immunity for every technology provider or for a person’s own content or conduct.

      
United States: copyright intermediary protections
17 U.S.C. §512(a)–(d), (i) and (m) provides conditional copyright liability limits for distinct functions such as transmission, caching, hosting and linking. Requirements depend on the function; applicable policies, technical measures, notice handling and designated-agent requirements matter. Merely displaying this disclaimer, not charging money, or operating a peer network does not establish eligibility. See the U.S. Copyright Office’s §512 guidance.

      
United States: distributing peer software
MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd., 545 U.S. 913 (2005) distinguishes lawful technology distribution from conduct intentionally encouraging infringement. A decentralized design or lawful uses do not provide blanket protection against liability for inducement. This demonstration is offered for lawful uses and does not authorize or encourage infringement.

      
European Union: intermediary roles
Digital Services Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, Articles 4–6, 8 and 9 distinguishes transmission, caching and hosting, with different conditions for liability exemptions. Article 8 addresses general monitoring duties; it does not eliminate obligations concerning specific lawful orders or other applicable duties. A browser storage node, relay, static host and content publisher do not necessarily have the same legal role.

      
These examples do not replace local law or legal advice, and do not assert that U.S. or EU law governs every participant. Obtain qualified advice for your jurisdiction before relying on a legal protection or deploying this software as an ongoing service. Mandatory rights and duties cannot be removed by calling software a demonstration.

    

    
Warranty and liability disclaimer
To the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, the demonstration is provided as is and as available, without warranties of fitness for a particular purpose, uninterrupted availability, security, confidentiality, non-infringement or data preservation. Its authors and static-page operator disclaim liability for participant-controlled content, independent third-party conduct, and loss, corruption, disclosure or unavailability arising from use of the demonstration, to the extent such liability may lawfully be excluded.
Nothing here excludes liability that applicable law does not allow to be excluded, removes statutory duties, limits non-waivable rights, or guarantees a defense to any claim. Liability is determined by applicable law and the facts, not by this notice alone. Reading this notice is not a substitute for obtaining necessary rights or complying with a lawful obligation.

    
Review the code and control your participation
Use Download source to inspect the raw deployed index.html; it contains application code, not an export of your room or browser data. Use Privacy settings to restrict direct connections, Browser storage to inspect local data, and the seeding/capture controls to stop your own contribution. These controls cannot erase files already saved by other people.
This notice describes this implementation and provides general information. It is not jurisdiction-specific legal advice or a certification of compliance. External legal references open only when you choose to follow them.
